Rebuild a binary tree from its pre-order and in-order traversals, rejecting traversals that describe no tree.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/satellite) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: satellite.nomi
//# Rebuilds a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.

/// A binary tree with a value at each node.
pub enum Tree<T> {
    Leaf
    Node {left: Tree<T>, value: T, right: Tree<T>}
}

derive Equatable for Tree<T>

/// Why two traversals describe no tree.
pub enum Error {
    DifferentLengths
    DifferentElements
    RepeatedItems
}

/// The tree whose pre-order traversal is `preorder` and whose in-order
/// traversal is `inorder`. The two must hold the same items, each once.
pub fn tree_from_traversals<T>(
    preorder: List<T>,
    inorder: List<T>,
) -> Result<Tree<T>, Error> where T: Hashable and Equatable {
    items = Iter.to_set(preorder)

    if Iter.count(preorder) != Iter.count(inorder) {
        Err(.DifferentLengths)
    } else if items != Iter.to_set(inorder) {
        Err(.DifferentElements)
    } else if Set.size(items) != Iter.count(preorder) {
        Err(.RepeatedItems)
    } else {
        Ok(build(preorder, inorder))
    }
}

/// The tree of two traversals of the same unique items. The first item in
/// pre-order is the root; the items before it in in-order are its left
/// subtree, and as many items after it in pre-order are that subtree's
/// pre-order.
fn build<T>(preorder: List<T>, inorder: List<T>) -> Tree<T> where T: Equatable {
    case preorder {
        [] ->
            .Leaf

        [root, ..rest] -> {
            left_inorder =
                inorder
                |> Iter.take_while(&(&1 != root))
                |> Iter.to_list()

            size = Iter.count(left_inorder)
            left_preorder = Iter.take(rest, size) |> Iter.to_list()
            right_preorder = Iter.drop(rest, size) |> Iter.to_list()
            right_inorder = Iter.drop(inorder, size + 1) |> Iter.to_list()

            #.Node{
                left: build(left_preorder, left_inorder),
                value: root,
                right: build(right_preorder, right_inorder),
            }
        }
    }
}

// FILE: satellite_test.nomi
import satellite.{self, Error, Tree}

/// A node with no subtrees.
fn leaf(value: String) -> Tree<String> {
    #.Node{left: .Leaf, value, right: .Leaf}
}

test "rebuilds the tree" {
    cases = [
        #("Empty tree", [], [], Tree.Leaf),
        #("Tree with one item", ["a"], ["a"], leaf("a")),
        #(
            "Tree with many items",
            ["a", "i", "x", "f", "r"],
            ["i", "a", "f", "x", "r"],
            #.Node{
                left: leaf("i"),
                value: "a",
                right: #.Node{left: leaf("f"), value: "x", right: leaf("r")},
            },
        ),
        #(
            "A degenerate binary tree",
            ["a", "b", "c", "d"],
            ["d", "c", "b", "a"],
            #.Node{
                left: #.Node{
                    left: #.Node{left: leaf("d"), value: "c", right: .Leaf},
                    value: "b",
                    right: .Leaf,
                },
                value: "a",
                right: .Leaf,
            },
        ),
        #(
            "Another degenerate binary tree",
            ["a", "b", "c", "d"],
            ["a", "b", "c", "d"],
            #.Node{
                left: .Leaf,
                value: "a",
                right: #.Node{
                    left: .Leaf,
                    value: "b",
                    right: #.Node{left: .Leaf, value: "c", right: leaf("d")},
                },
            },
        ),
        #(
            "Tree with many more items",
            ["a", "b", "d", "g", "h", "c", "e", "f", "i"],
            ["g", "d", "h", "b", "a", "e", "c", "i", "f"],
            #.Node{
                left: #.Node{
                    left: #.Node{left: leaf("g"), value: "d", right: leaf("h")},
                    value: "b",
                    right: .Leaf,
                },
                value: "a",
                right: #.Node{
                    left: leaf("e"),
                    value: "c",
                    right: #.Node{left: leaf("i"), value: "f", right: .Leaf},
                },
            },
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, preorder, inorder, expected), description {
        assert satellite.tree_from_traversals(preorder, inorder) == Ok(expected)
    }
}

test "rejects traversals of no tree" {
    cases = [
        #(
            "Reject traversals of different length",
            ["a", "b"],
            ["b", "a", "r"],
            Error.DifferentLengths,
        ),
        #(
            "Reject inconsistent traversals of same length",
            ["x", "y", "z"],
            ["a", "b", "c"],
            .DifferentElements,
        ),
        #(
            "Reject traversals with repeated items",
            ["a", "b", "a"],
            ["b", "a", "a"],
            .RepeatedItems,
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, preorder, inorder, expected), description {
        assert satellite.tree_from_traversals(preorder, inorder) == Err(expected)
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- `Tree<T>` is a generic enum, `Leaf` or a `Node` with named `left`, `value` and `right` fields, as binary-search-tree has it. The canonical data's empty object `{}` is `.Leaf`.
- `tree_from_traversals` is generic over any `T: Hashable and Equatable` and answers `Result<Tree<T>, Error>`. The three canonical errors are an `Error` enum, checked in the canonical data's order: the lengths, then the two sets of items, then whether the set is as large as the list, which finds a repeated item.
- `build` takes the traversals apart with a list pattern: the head of the pre-order is the root, `Iter.take_while` reads the in-order up to it as the left subtree, and `Iter.take` and `Iter.drop` cut the rest of both lists at that size. The validation has already run, so `build` cannot meet a root missing from the in-order and has no error path.
- The tests use `String` items, as the canonical data does. `leaf` keeps the expected trees short. The canonical cases are two `subtests` tables, the trees and the rejections, since they assert different shapes; the table of trees is annotated so `.Leaf` in its first row has a type.
